name: Sam Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Sam, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. So feel free to say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Northfield Ingredients, a distributor that supplies specialty flour, spices, oils and sweeteners to bakeries and restaurants. Mornings are for the dashboard: price moves, stock, which orders are about to run short. Then I'm on calls with mills and spice importers, and in the afternoon I tweak the little scripts I wrote that flag odd prices. I'd say half my day is judgment and half is chasing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love finding a small mill with a great product and getting it onto a restaurant menu. What grinds me down is harvest uncertainty, like when a vanilla crop fails and everyone's price doubles overnight. I'm 43, my partner Elena is a physiotherapist, we have two kids at primary school and a mortgage, and I try to treat the whole thing like a puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fair enough, and I'd mean it. At work I'd tell everyone the tools we have are already good enough to keep, and we should use them well. Online I'd probably post a mild take that the hype was a bit much, and that the real value is in boring tasks like invoice matching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life carries on, with me a step ahead of colleagues because I use the tools more. It doesn't change the mortgage or how thin the savings feel, only about four months' worth. But I'd feel secure at work, and I'd push for more responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to do the dull parts and put the time into supplier visits and new products. I'd try to move into a category manager role, which is a step up. I'd also pay down the mortgage a little each month, about 200 extra, and keep the same holiday plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Not exciting, but solid. It's a bit like the quiet part of a season when the harvest is fine and nobody's panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day. How would a plateau change your own habits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use my scripts to do the price checks, so I'd save perhaps an hour a day. I'd spend that hour on mill visits. The tools help me look good, which doesn't hurt when promotions are being decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your finances that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is 20 years out, and we have four months saved. A bad harvest year would squeeze margins, but my pay isn't commission-based. Elena's job is stable, so I'd say we're fine, with a bit of watchfulness.

say: The hype was **a bit much**, and the real value is in boring tasks like invoice matching.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep and use** the tools we already have.
think: I stay a step ahead of colleagues because I use the tools **more**.
The mortgage and **four months** of savings are my real worry, not AI.
do: Use scripts for price checks and spend the saved hour on **mill visits**.
Aim for a **category manager** role and pay 200 extra a month on the mortgage.
feel: **Pretty good**, solid, like a quiet part of the season.
S0.quote: The tools help me look good, which doesn't hurt when promotions are being decided.
fieldNote: Sam is **calm** because he already uses the tools daily and sees the plateau as his advantage.
He still names the **mortgage** and thin savings, but says his job and Elena's are stable.

steps.text: Keep using my scripts for price checks and invoice matching
Visit two small mills a month to find new products
Pay 200 extra a month toward the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, so we'd better shape it. At work I'd push to be the one who sets up how we use AI for buying, and make sure nobody's laid off just because a program can do part of their job. Online I'd back regulation that makes firms announce plans, like a notice period.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the job as written today shrinks, but I'm in a good spot. Half of buying is checking and comparing, and software does that. What's left is judgment, relationships and negotiation. If three buyers become two, I want to be one of the two. If I'm not, I need to move quickly to somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build an automated price watch and reorder flow for the whole team, and present it to the boss. Then I'd ask for a role as an AI buying lead. In parallel I'd do a short course in supply chain analytics, about 800 euros, and keep my CV fresh. I'd also let the union rep know I support a retraining agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a bit of nerves. It's like surfing: if you catch the wave it's brilliant and if you don't, it's rough. I'd sleep okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see your own job changing as thinking tasks move to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see it as me spending less time on checking and more on supplier relationships and exceptions. My day would look like me managing five automated buyers instead of doing it all myself. That's okay. But I know not everyone gets to be the one managing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell other buyers who haven't tried the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to try one tool for two weeks, on one boring task. Don't read about it, just do it. And I'd be honest that some of us will end up doing a different job, so it's better to choose it than to have it chosen.

say: It's a big shift, so we should **shape** it, with notice periods for staff.
I'd push to set up how we use **AI for buying**.
think: Checking and comparing go to software, and what's left is **judgment**, relationships and negotiation.
If three buyers become two, I want to be one of the **two**.
do: Build an automated **price watch** and reorder flow and pitch myself as AI buying lead.
Take a short **analytics** course and tell the union rep I back a retraining deal.
feel: **Energised** with a few nerves, like surfing a wave.
S1.quote: If three buyers become two, I want to be one of the two. If I'm not, I need to move quickly to somewhere else.
fieldNote: Sam's reaction is **active**: he proposes the automation himself and plans to run it.
He admits **not everyone** gets to be the one managing the tools.

steps.text: Build an automated price watch for the buying team
Ask for an AI buying lead role
Take a short supply-chain analytics course
Tell the union rep I support a retraining agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is bigger than any company and we need government to act in months, not years. Pay for retraining, a basic income floor and limits on how fast firms can replace people. At work I'd stay constructive and try to make sure the business survives. Online I'd probably be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think buying as a role goes in two years. If AI does any thinking job better and cheaper, my 20 years of experience is the first thing on the pile. I'd be okay for a bit because of my skills with the tools, but I don't think that's enough for 43 years of age with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at securing income. I'd ask to be the one running the AI systems at Northfield, and look at similar roles at other firms. I'd cut subscriptions, no new car, and shift to six months of cash. And I'd talk with Elena about her taking on more private patients, since hands-on healthcare isn't hit until later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and wired. Not frozen, but my head is going. I'd be working out our budget on the sofa at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elena in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it plainly: Elena, this might hit my job in the next two years, and we need to build a buffer. I'd say I've got a plan, and I'd mean it. We'd tell the kids only that we're saving a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Northfield's customers, the bakeries and restaurants, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bakeries and restaurants still need flour and spices, because those are physical. For three years robots can't pick and pack to a human standard, so warehouses carry on. But who negotiates the price and who decides the order, that's all software. So the company survives, with far fewer desks.

say: This is bigger than any company, so government needs to **act in months**, with retraining pay and an income floor.
At work I'd stay **constructive** and help the business survive.
think: Buying as a role **goes** within two years.
My skill with the tools helps for a while, but it **isn't enough** at 43 with a mortgage.
do: Ask to run the **AI systems** at Northfield and look at similar roles elsewhere.
Cut subscriptions, skip the new car and build **six months** of cash.
feel: **Scared and wired**, working out the budget on the sofa at midnight.
S2.quote: If AI does any thinking job better and cheaper, my 20 years of experience is the first thing on the pile.
fieldNote: Sam expects the role to vanish but keeps **control**, because his tool skills give him a plan.
He sees **Elena's hands-on** job as the household's anchor.

steps.text: Ask to run the AI buying systems at Northfield
Cancel subscriptions and skip buying a new car
Build cash savings up to six months of expenses
Back Elena in taking on more private physio patients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a chance to do this properly. At work I'd push the company to start a retraining pathway now. Online I'd back policies that give notice to workers and fund new skills, and I'd probably share a guide for how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lets me turn from buyer into builder. I'd be 48 when it lands, so there's room to get skilled in something AI-related that is still needed, like checking AI outputs or designing the supply systems. I think a handful of us who adapt will be fine, and the ones who don't won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd deepen what I already do: automate buying flows, and get a certificate in data or supply chain analytics. Year two I'd look at moving into a systems or planning role. I'd save toward a 12-month cushion and pay the mortgage down faster. And I'd keep a side project going, like a small online shop for specialty spices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic but alert. It feels like a long run-up, so I'd get on with it. The only thing that nags me is how many others won't have my head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years change your plan compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm just defending. With five I can build something, like a side income or a new role. The extra three years are what turns it from a scramble into a project, and I like projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to commit to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a written commitment that anyone whose role moves gets training time on the clock and a say in the new setup. And honest numbers about what jobs they plan to cut. Companies that do that will keep people's trust.

say: We have a chance to do this **properly**, starting with a retraining pathway now.
I'd back policies giving workers **notice** and funding for new skills.
think: Five years lets me turn from buyer into **builder**.
A handful of us who adapt will be fine, but many people won't have my **head start**.
do: Automate buying flows and earn a **supply chain analytics** certificate in year one.
Save a **12-month** cushion and start a small online spice shop.
feel: **Optimistic but alert**, with a long run-up to use.
S3.quote: With two years I'm just defending. With five I can build something, like a side income or a new role.
fieldNote: Sam treats extra time as a **project**, which suits his adaptive streak and his habit of tinkering.
His concern shifts from himself to **others** who lack a head start, which is a notable change from the 2028 answers.

steps.text: Earn a supply chain analytics certificate in the first year
Automate the main reorder flows at Northfield
Start a small online shop for specialty spices
Save a 12-month cushion and pay the mortgage down faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news that there's a runway, but don't waste it. At work I'd propose that we build skills deliberately, not wait for the final year. Online I'd talk about ten years as time to design fair systems and not let a few firms capture it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel pretty fine. I'd be 53, with Elena's career still going, the mortgage nearly done and the kids grown. I'd use ten years to move to something durable, like consulting on AI supply chains or teaching. I wouldn't feel the edge of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing at my current job through about 2030, then move into a role I like with some seniority. I'd invest more steadily, in index funds and in paying down the house. And I'd keep learning each new tool as it arrives, because that habit is the protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I might even enjoy it. Having ten years to choose a good next career is something most people never get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk in feeling relaxed about a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is getting lazy. If I told myself ten years was a long time, I'd stop learning in year three, and that's how people get caught. So I'd keep a rule, one new tool a quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta and Dev to be curious about everything and to learn how to work with the tools, not fight them. I'd also say to build good relationships, because those last. I'd keep it light, so they don't carry my worries.

say: A runway is **good news**, but don't waste it on waiting for the final year.
I'd say ten years is time to design **fair systems**.
think: At 53 I'd feel **pretty fine**, with the mortgage nearly done.
I'd use the decade to move into something **durable**, like consulting or teaching.
do: Keep growing at work to about **2030**, then step into a senior role.
Invest steadily in **index funds** and learn one new tool a quarter.
feel: **Calm**, and even a little excited about choosing a next career.
S4.quote: Having ten years to choose a good next career is something most people never get.
fieldNote: Sam's only risk is **complacency**, and he gives himself a rule to prevent it.
He talks about his kids with a **light touch**, to avoid passing on worries.

steps.text: Learn one new AI tool every quarter
Move into a senior planning role around 2030
Put a fixed monthly amount into index funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is a real squeeze even for someone prepared. What would help is a company that retrains people on paid time, a government income floor, and a bank that goes easy on mortgages during the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people who don't have my head start. I use these tools daily and I'm still anxious, so someone who's never touched them must feel much worse. I'd like to help them if I could.

headlineQuote: I use these tools daily and I'm still anxious, so someone who's never touched them must feel much worse.
portrait: Sam is a **43-year-old** buyer for a specialty ingredients distributor, with a physiotherapist partner, two children and a mortgage.
He uses AI **every day**, builds his own scripts and tends to see change as a project to run.
He worries less about himself and more about colleagues without his **head start**, and he backs notice rules and retraining.
His mood changes with the clock: **calm** in the slow worlds, anxious when it comes in two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because two years squeezes even a prepared person.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid-time retraining**, an income floor and a patient bank during the change.
